planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Josee is a compact, reblooming lilac that flowers heavily in spring with lighter repeat flushes through summer.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and deadhead spent flower clusters right after the main spring flush to encourage rebloom. Josee bears fragrant lavender-pink flower clusters in a heavy spring display, then continues producing lighter flushes of bloom through summer into fall, an unusual trait for lilac, which typically flowers only once. Its compact, dense habit fits smaller gardens and foundation plantings better than large old-fashioned lilac shrubs. Like most lilacs it needs a real winter chill to flower well and performs best in the cooler end of its hardiness range rather than the mildest Gulf South winters. Established shrubs are long-lived and low-maintenance, needing only post-bloom deadheading and occasional renewal pruning of the oldest canes.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; Lavender Lady is a low-chill lilac cultivar specifically bred to flower reliably in mild-winter climates where most lilacs fail to bloom.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and deadhead spent flower clusters right after bloom since next year's buds set soon after. Lavender Lady was bred in California specifically to solve the problem that most lilac cultivars require far more winter chill than mild climates provide, and it is one of the most reliable lilacs for flowering without a hard, extended winter, producing fragrant lavender-purple flower clusters in spring even in the milder end of zone 9. It is one of the few lilac cultivars genuinely suited to Gulf South gardens, where standard Syringa vulgaris cultivars often fail to bud out or bloom weakly for lack of chill hours. Established shrubs are long-lived, needing only post-bloom deadheading and occasional renewal pruning of the oldest canes to stay vigorous.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Low-Chill Lilac Cultivars

common_name: Angel White Wisteria (Long-Raceme White Chinese Wisteria)

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, pergola, or arbor built to support a mature vine's substantial weight.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy support structure. Angel White bears long, hanging racemes of pure white, lightly fragrant flowers in spring, a striking alternative to the more familiar lavender-purple wisteria colors, on the same vigorous, fast-growing twining vine typical of Chinese wisteria. Because Wisteria sinensis is considered invasive in many Eastern and Gulf South states, capable of escaping cultivation and overwhelming native vegetation, site it carefully away from natural areas and be prepared for regular pruning to control its aggressive spread — gardeners seeking a similar look with a well-behaved habit may prefer the native Wisteria frutescens instead. Prune hard after flowering and again in late winter to control size and encourage flower bud formation on short spurs rather than rampant vegetative growth.
